pr_title: [Python] Caching DBInstances and sharing them over multiple connections
pr_body:
The idea is to cache database instances for connections created over the same db file.
That means that different write connections should be able to connect to a file, with the MVCC taking care of any updates underneath.
The only downside of sharing a database instance is that both connections must have the same configuration, if they have different configurations, then I throw an error.

Fix: #4017
pr_comments: After some discussion with @hawkfish regarding the ODBC driver running into the same problem - I am thinking we perhaps want to do this in the general database connection API instead. That way all clients will support this behavior in the same manner. @pdet @hannes thoughts?
I think that makes sense, I'm happy to move this a layer up

One issue that would then remain then is the double loading of the Pandas scan/Map functions.  I think that can be solved nicely by wrapping those functions into an extension (e.g. `PythonAPIExtension`, `RAPIExtension` for the R DataFrame scan, etc). That way the extension can always be loaded after connecting - as the system will simply not load an extension more than once.

I am not such a fan of those lists of databases, we used to have this in the past and it was a long source of issues. Why don't we change the API so that its more natural to connect to existing instances instead? Overall, the pain here comes from existing db apis being designed around client/server where no singleton instance needs to be managed. I fear there is no great overall solution, for R we stuffed the instance into the driver object, maybe that's also an option for ODBC. For Python, we could just have duckdb.instance(dbdir) that offers a connect() or something like that. It will need to be carefully considered by API I fear.

Changing the API sounds nicer indeed but I don't think that is a complete solution, since as you mentioned all the existing database API's are designed around client-server. We could try to push our own custom API, but that will likely still let many users run into this issue when they try to use it through an existing API, and won't help resolve the issues we run into with existing tools (e.g. Tableau not working).

I think the complete solutions are either (1) we add this list of databases and seamlessly connect the user to an existing instance if it exists, or (2) we go the SQLite route and allow different database systems to connect to the same file, also for write workloads. (2) is more versatile but implies a lot of changes and restrictions placed on our existing code base, such as e.g. getting rid of the buffer manager and any forms of in-memory caching and rewriting the storage layer to account for multiple concurrent processes attaching to the same database.

Could you perhaps expand on the set of issues you ran into with this feature in the past? Were they related to the implementation of the feature, or to the general behavior causing surprising behavior for users?

I think we have a quite clean implementation here with a set of weak pointers and a lock. Database instances will be cleaned up as usual if there are no more references to them and everything will be entirely thread-safe. The way I would envision this is we have a define that toggles this behavior (`DUCKDB_ENABLE_CONNECTION_CACHE`) that is enabled for certain clients (e.g. the Python, R, ODBC, JDBC clients).

Let's discuss tomorrow with @hannes , I think we want this functionality in the base library with some caveats (e.g. it should be opt-in with an explicit define, e.g. `DUCKDB_ENABLE_CONNECTION_CACHE`).
Closing this PR after a discussion on a more generic solution.

issue_context.title: Python commits from same thread, but different connections make unexpected results.
issue_context.body:
#### What happens?
When two python connections, form the same thread and process, commit two new tables, one is overwritten. My expectation is that both tables appear, since there is no conflict.

#### To Reproduce

```
# make a new db
duckdb /tmp/tmp.ddb -c "create table X (a int)";
```

Given an existing `/tmp/tmp.ddb` with no tables.
```
nursa@Nicholass-MacBook-Air ~ % python
Python 3.9.11 (main, Apr 10 2022, 10:19:17)
[Clang 13.1.6 (clang-1316.0.21.2)] on darwin
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>> import duckdb
>>> con1 = duckdb.connect("/tmp/tmp.ddb")
>>> con2 = duckdb.connect("/tmp/tmp.ddb")
>>> con1.execute("CREATE TABLE foo1 as SELECT 1 as a, 2 as b")
<duckdb.DuckDBPyConnection object at 0x1008f3b70>
>>> con1.commit()
<duckdb.DuckDBPyConnection object at 0x1008f3b70>
>>> con2.execute("CREATE TABLE bar1 as SELECT 2 as a, 3 as b")
<duckdb.DuckDBPyConnection object at 0x1008f5bf0>
>>> con2.commit()
<duckdb.DuckDBPyConnection object at 0x1008f5bf0>
>>> con2.close()
>>> con1.close()
>>> con3 = duckdb.connect("/tmp/tmp.ddb")
>>> con3.execute("select * from information_schema.tables").fetchall()
[(None, 'main', 'bar1', 'BASE TABLE', None, None, None, None, None, 'YES', 'NO', None)]
>>>
```

This shows that `con2` has overwritten the table created by `con1` even though `con1` committed.

~~My expectation is that the second connection, which was opened writeable, should throw an exception as soon as the connection attempt is made to the same path.~~
My expectation is to see both tables.

#### Environment (please complete the following information):
 - OS: OS X 12.3.1 
 - DuckDB Version: v0.4.0
 - DuckDB Client: python

#### Identity Disclosure:
 - Full Name:  Nicholas Ursa
 - Affiliation: MotherDuck Corp.


#### Before Submitting

- [X] **Have you tried this on the latest `master` branch?**
* **Python**: `pip install duckdb --upgrade --pre`
` Downloading duckdb-0.4.1.dev188-cp39-cp39-macosx_11_0_arm64.whl (13.5 MB)`
- [X] **Have you tried the steps to reproduce? Do they include all relevant data and configuration? Does the issue you report still appear there?**
